## Setting up

- At <https://ondemand.osc.edu>, start a new RStudio session
  ([Starting an RStudio Server session at OSC](../week11/w11a_r-basics.html#starting-an-rstudio-server-session-at-osc))

- Switch to your `week11` RStudio Project
  ([Working directory and RStudio Projects](../week11/w11a_r-basics.html#Working-directory-and-RStudio-Projects))
  
- Open a new R script in RStudio:
  `File` -> `New File` -> `R Script` and save the R script as 
  `w11_exercises.R` (inside `week11`).
   You will write your answers to the exercises below in this R script.

## Part A: Create variables and perfrom arithmetic operations

1. Assign the value `5` to the variable `week11`, and `10` to the variable `week12`.
   Print these variables to the console.

2. Add the values of `week11` and `week12` and assign the result to to a new variable `total_weeks`.
   Similarly, multiply the values of `week11` and `week12` and assign the result
   to a new variable `multiplied_weeks`.
   Print these variables to the console.

## Part B: Create vectors and name its elements

3. Create a vector `v1` that contains the numbers 1 through 5.
   Then, extract the third element of `v1`, printing it to the console.
   Likewise, create another variable `v2` with numbers 6 to 10.
   Check what data types `v1` and `v2` contain.

4. Change the name of the third element of `v1` to "Midweek" and print `v1`.
   Check the data type of `v1` after changing third element to `Midweek`.
   Try to change the `v1` to `numeric` and see what happens.

5. Create a vector `v3` that combines `v1` and `v2`.
   Extract the third, fourth and fifth element of `v3` and assign it to `v4`.
   Print `v4` to the console.

## Part C: Install and load new packages in R

6. Install the package `palmerpenguins` and load the package in R.
   We will use this package in `week13` for data visualization.

## Part D: Working with matrix and dataframes

7. Look for help for `matrix` function and create a matrix with numbers 1 to 10 with 2 rows and 5 columns
    and assign it to a new object called `my_matrix`.

8. Last week we worked with the `iris` data frame,
   which is one of the data sets that comes with R.
   For this exercise, we will use the `mtcars` data frame, which similarly comes with R.
   Start by storing `mtcars` in a new object called `my_cars`,
   then view the first 6 rows of `my_cars`.

9. Check the structure of the `my_cars` data frame.
   Structure of data shows the datatypes of different variables in the data frame.
   Compute the mean of the `mpg` variable of `my_cars` data frame.

10. Show the first 6 rows of the `my_cars` data frame. 
    Select columns `mpg`, `cyl`, and `hp` from the `my_cars` data frame and display the first 6 rows.

    ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
    Remember to load the _tidyverse_ package before using the `select()` function.
    :::

11. Write a single "pipeline" that manipulates `my_cars` by:
    - Selecting columns `mpg` (miles per gallon) and `cyl` (number of cylinders)
    - Only keeping rows with `mpg` greater than 10 and `cyl` equal to 6.
    - Renaming the `cyl` column to `cylinders`
    - Assigning the resulting data frame to an object called `my_cars_filtered`
  
12. Save the new_data frame as a CSV file called `my_cars_filtered.csv` in your working directory.
    In the RStudio "Files" pane,
    check that the file is there and click on it to view it in the editor pane.

## Solutions

### Part A: Create variables and perform arithmetic operations

<details><summary>**1.** Assign values to variables</summary>


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
week11 <- 5
week11
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
[1] 5
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
week12 <- 10
week12
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
[1] 10
```


:::
:::

</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Arithmetic operations</summary>


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
total_weeks <- week11 + week12
total_weeks
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
[1] 15
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
multiplied_weeks <- week11 * week12
multiplied_weeks
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
[1] 50
```


:::
:::

</details>

### Part B: Create and name a vector

<details><summary>**3.** Create vectors and extract elements</summary>


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

v1[3]
```



:::

```{.r .cell-code}

str(v1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output

```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str(v2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output

```


:::
:::

</details>

<details><summary>**4.** Change vectors </summary>

**After replacing a numeric element with a string, the entire vector becomes a character vector**
**And when you try to convert it back to numeric, R will return `NA` for the non-numeric elements:**
   

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
v1[3] <- "Midweek"
v1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
[1] "1"       "2"       "Midweek" "4"       "5"      
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str(v1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output
 chr [1:5] "1" "2" "Midweek" "4" "5"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
as.numeric(v1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

``` warning-r-output
Warning: NAs introduced by coercion
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output

```


:::
:::

</details>

<details><summary>**5.** Combine vectors </summary>


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

v4 <- v3[3:5]
v4
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

``` regular-r-output

```


:::
:::


### Part C: Install and load new packages in R

<details><summary>**6.** Install and load a package </summary>
